text: Amrita Ghulati: ...for joining the second edition of In Focus. We started last month, and I think it was a very well-received initiative, and we're encouraged to continue. In fact, we have presenters lined up until November. So, very excited to bring all the great work that's happening within the community, by the community, to the community, for the community. And today we have with us Devesh and Himansshu from two different organizations, both committed to student success in different ways.

Amrita Ghulati: We're going to have Devesh start and talk to us about Futurowise, which is essentially a platform and a sort of—I shouldn't say the word platform—which is essentially an organization that's enabling students to explore emerging fields, develop practical skills, and build portfolios through project-based learning experiences. So, really seeing the applied side of education and concepts that they see and read about in class.

Amrita Ghulati: And after him, we'll have Himansshu Jainn from The Student Scoop, that runs an organization helping students navigate the demands of international curricula through personalized academic mentoring and structured learning support. And we got both of them together because one is consolidating on what's happening in the classroom, and there's another organization that's trying to build a little further away on strong academic skills, and essentially complimenting each other's work.

Amrita Ghulati: So, thank you for joining, and we will have Devesh share a little bit about the work in the first 15 minutes, followed perhaps by Q&A—we'll take a call then—or else we'll move straight away to The Student Scoop with Himansshu, and then do Q&A together, seeing how we all sort of go through the process, right? So, over to you, Devesh.

Devesh Lahoti: Fantastic. Thank you so much, Amrita. First of all, thank you for envisioning In Focus. Thank you, Bijoya, Bhakti, for this opportunity, and thank you to all of you for being here today, showing up. I'm excited, thrilled to share about Futurowise with you. I have known many of you for the last many, many years, and you know my work with the NextGenius Scholarship Program for the last decade. And while working with the scholarship program, and while reviewing hundreds and hundreds of applications, I realized that there were two things which stood out when we separated the scholarship winners with those who did not win a scholarship. And that was their curiosity and independent thinking.

Devesh Lahoti: And when I dug deeper upon it, when I thought more about it, I realized that there—you know, after looking at the whole ecosystem—I realized that there was a need of a program like Futurowise, which brought forward both their curiosity and independent thinking. And last year, in 2025, Futurowise was launched.

Devesh Lahoti: What Futurowise is—it's a program which—Futurowise is, you know, I would like to say platform—the platform which prepares students for—high school students for the future skills through short, intensive online courses on skills which are important for the next decade. Every program that we run is led by industry experts and professors, and students leave with a real skill and a published project and a certificate—all of that within a 2- to 4-week program.

Devesh Lahoti: So, to encapsulate, what we do is we run short online courses—and when I say short, these are 2- to 4-week-long courses—which are taught by professors from the university or industry experts. And the kind of students that we find ourselves working with are typically curious, academically inclined, and want to learn a future skill. And that's what we do. When a student finishes their program, when a student completes their program with us, they end up with a future skill.

Devesh Lahoti: And we are seeing the world around us. Everything, the pace of change is tremendous. AI is changing the way we work. Geopolitics are, you know, disrupting everything around us. Robotics and automation is changing the way jobs are done. And through Futurowise, we are now helping students develop those skills which are going to be important in the next decade.

Devesh Lahoti: Every student develops a new skill. They create a project, and this is where, you know, this is where the independent thing bit comes in. When you work with us, you work by yourself. We teach you the skills through online sessions, and we help you create a project which is then published on our platform. And again, this is something—publishing your work is something which really adds value to your profiles when you are applying to colleges. And finally, you earn a certificate. So every student who works with Futurowise, they develop a future skill, they create a project, they publish their work on our platform, and they earn a certificate.

Devesh Lahoti: I'll show you some of the programs which are coming up over the next 3 to 4 months. And each and every one of these programs are designed with a vision of ensuring that this is a skill that will help them in the next decade. And I have like a small list here, but there are more programs that we are working on: 1. Foundations of Money and Investing: which is what teaches the students about how money works, how finances work, and how to build—how to invest your money. And eventually, every student ends with a virtual portfolio of their own. 2. Foundations of Data Science: and this is one of my favorites. The cohort is running right now, and the next cohort starts in August—end of August. And in Foundations of Data Science, students are learning Tableau, which is a data visualization tool. They are learning a little bit of Python, and they're learning how data science works, how to gather the data, how to analyze the data, how to visualize the data, and finally how to make a whole story out of that data. And students are working on their own projects. Interesting projects—I was just in conversation with some students—they are working on how literacy rates across different states changed over the last decade and does gender have a role to play in that. Very interesting topic. 3. Prompt Engineering: is starting 4th of July, and I have shared the flyer with some of you over WhatsApp. Prompt engineering is a 2-week program where you learn how AI works, you learn how to develop beautiful prompts which will give you the right kind of results. It'll tell you about the ethical aspects of AI, and eventually you will close with your own project in prompt engineering which will help you design your own study plan or something like that. 4. Foundations of Agentic AI: It's happening over the Independence Day weekend, 15th and 16th of August, where students will work with us to develop their own AI agents. It's exciting, and I think if you have your students, you can give them projects like "Why don't you build this AI agent for me?" And by the end of this program, they will bring that project to you, which might help you in your own work—a real AI agent. 5. Foundations of Entrepreneurship: is about creating your own business plan, which happens in October—October 2, 3, 4—where students will be with us over a weekend, and they will learn the basics, the foundations of entrepreneurship. They will learn the tools which entrepreneurs use, and eventually they will build their own business plan. 6. Brand Strategy and Digital Marketing: is a program where you learn about how brands work. And in a few weeks, I'll host a session for all of you, like a masterclass on digital marketing and brand strategy. Just look out for that invite. We'll talk about how you can build your own brand, and you can also start digital marketing by yourself.

Devesh Lahoti: Those are some of the programs which are coming up. A very simple structure of how it all works: - Step 1: You go to our website—it's futurowise.com (f-u-t-u-r-o-w-i-s-e.com)—you select a program and you register. - Step 2: Once you do that, you see that you are invited to all of these online sessions that we host on Zoom. So students join these online workshops, online sessions. And all programs are done in small groups. You know, typically the group size is about 15 students—15, not more than 20 ever. So something of this kind of a group. All students are required to keep their cameras on, which ensures engagement—each and every one of them. All students are required to join on time, or you don't get your attendance, and all students are required to submit their assignments. So that all ensures that they are learning that skill, which is critical. They attend these online sessions, which are taught by experts, industry experts—CEO, CXO-level people—or professors with decades of experience. - Step 3: Then they work on their assignments, they work on their projects, they submit it to us. Not I, but the professors give them feedback on their submissions. They talk about how the project—you know, they give feedback things like why something is unrealistic, why what they have assumed might not work, things like that. It's a genuine feedback that they give to the students. The students then work on that feedback and rework and resubmit their work to publish on our platform.

Himansshu Jainn: Thank you so much, Amrita. Thanks, Bhakti. Thanks, Bijoya, for this opportunity. I think as a whole, it's going to be a great learning for me as well at this moment. One second, ma'am.
Himansshu Jainn: [silence/screen sharing setup]

Himansshu Jainn: Right. So in the meantime, I just have Tanay from my team who's just going to be sharing the screen. So once again, good evening to everyone, and thank you for joining in and sparing some time with us. I am Himansshu Jainn, I'm the founder of The Student Scoop.

Himansshu Jainn: Today I'm going to be spending some time not here to just present what The Student Scoop is just like any other academic support center, but I'm going to be talking about a very specific gap that primarily affects counselors, school leaders, university partners, parents, and students. So the gap that I'm going to be addressing today is the academic execution. So our focus is very, very simple: How do we primarily help international curriculum students become academically stronger, more confident, and better prepared for global university pathways?

Himansshu Jainn: So let's focus on the core gap. As counselors, I'm sure we all have been doing a powerful job of giving students some direction. You guys have been helping with university strategy, course selection, application narratives, essays, and profile positioning. Schools have been doing the job of delivering the curriculum, classroom learning, grade progression. But between the counseling direction and the school curriculum, there has often been a gap, and that gap has been academic execution. And that is where The Student Scoop primarily operates.

Himansshu Jainn: So we work with students on diagnostic, concept mastery, exam practice, internal assessment, extended essay support, parent reporting, as well as academic evidence. So our belief is very, very simple: that counseling outcomes will become stronger only when the academic execution is visible, measurable, as well as aligned.

Himansshu Jainn: So what we see that as counselors or any other TOC members have already experienced—I'm sure many of you must have seen this pattern—that a student generally looks very ambitious on paper: they want to do medicine, they want to do engineering, economics, CS, or selective global universities, but the academic risk is often hidden until it's quite late.

Himansshu Jainn: Sometimes the risk is the subject selection: a student ends up choosing Higher Levels or Standard Levels or A-Level subjects without having enough evidence of the readiness for that subject. Sometimes it's also the parent anxiety: parents want clarity, but receive reassurance instead of measurable progress. And sometimes the profile story is very strong, but the marks, the IA, the EE, or the STEM evidence does not support that story.

Himansshu Jainn: So the practical question to you all is this: which student really needs academic intervention before counseling outcomes are compromised? The students end up losing momentum primarily when there is an academic risk that does not suddenly appear in Grade 12; it has actually built gradually: - In Grade 8, Grade 9, students move from recall-based learning to analysis, evaluation, and evidence-based responses. - In Grade 10, we see that IGCSE and Cambridge students face board pressure, exam techniques, subject-readiness decisions. - And likewise in Grade 11 and 12 with the IBDP, students' predicted grades, IAs, EEs, mocks, finals, application, and a lot of other habit and systems which are not in line with what they want.

Himansshu Jainn: And The Student Scoop primarily works with students if they are involved much, much before the panic stage. That is where the diagnostics, academic roadmaps, structured intervention can actually make a serious difference.

Himansshu Jainn: So just a quick brief about what The Student Scoop has been built as: we are primarily built as an academic execution partner for international curriculum students. Ma'am, can we just go to the previous slide? One more slide ahead, please. Yeah, thank you.

Himansshu Jainn: So The Student Scoop has primarily been a premium academic execution partner for international curriculum students: - 9+ years of academic execution experience. - Mentored about 1,000+ students across programs. - 3 of our Mumbai centers as well as with online academic support. - Our curriculum focus includes IBDP, IGCSE, MYP, Cambridge, as well as A-Levels. - Our subject support includes Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, and Economics.

Himansshu Jainn: But what makes us different is not just the subject teaching; it's the academic system behind the teaching. We start right at the diagnostic stage, do our topic tracking, categorize the homework, have a structured feedback loop in process, continuing with parent reporting as well as admissions alignment.

Himansshu Jainn: To our credibility, we have worked with various international schools in Mumbai, in India, as well as across a few countries as well. So we do have a good understanding of various international school ecosystems. So a student from an IB school or a Cambridge or an international ecosystem may need very, very different academic handling, and our strength lies in handling those set of students.

Himansshu Jainn: So we follow a very, very simple academic readiness engine—that is, the operating system behind which and how we support students. We follow a 5-stage roadmap: 1. Diagnose: Topic-wise diagnostic, concept gaps, and exam skill gaps. 2. Map: Roadmap by subject, board, school timeline, as well as the admissions goal. 3. Teach: Concept mastery with curriculum-specific pedagogy. 4. Practice: Homework tiers, exam-style questions, timed assessments. 5. Report: Parent clarity, counselor summary, and next-action plan.
Himansshu Jainn: So referral does not primarily just disappear into a class schedule coming from any counselor; it is actually entering into a monitored academic system.

Himansshu Jainn: So let me give you a few examples of what kind of student journey can we primarily support and what's the outcome you can expect: - A Grade 10 student moving into an IBDP program may need a subject-readiness diagnostic as well as bridge support. Outcome: Better subject clarity and smoother transition. - A Grade 11 IBDP student maybe struggling with a predicted grade might need concept repair, exam strategy, and parent tracking systems in place. Outcome: Improved academic confidence and structured grade recovery. - A STEM-focused student applying abroad may need project mentoring and academic profile building. Outcome: Stronger evidence for applications and interviews.
Himansshu Jainn: And our success is primarily not just measured by marks; it is measured by clarity, confidence, academic discipline, parent visibility, and better decision-making.

Himansshu Jainn: Some of our programs that can primarily be of good importance to each one of you in the room today: - If you spot any student having weak subject confidence: IB, IGCSE, MYP, Cambridge subject support. - If a student is transitioning from Grade 9 or Grade 10 into an IBDP or A-Levels course: Grade 9–10 to IBDP / A-Level bridge. - If predicted grades have been a concern: Crash course + mock review + grade recovery plan. - If profile depth is weak, especially for STEM-focused students: STEM research projects and real-world learning. - If parents are found to be anxious: Diagnostics, roadmap, and reporting.

Himansshu Jainn: So some of the case studies: - Use Case 1 (Grade 10 to IBDP): Let's say we have a Grade 10 student moving to the IBDP and wants to do engineering or medicine, economics or CS. The aspiration is very, very strong, but the subject choice may be driven just by ambition rather than readiness of the evidence that we have. The student may want to do Physics at the Higher Level, Chemistry at the Higher Levels, Math at the Higher Levels, but no one has properly diagnosed whether the student is ready for the academic jump. What we do is we run a 6- to 8-week bridge plan. We assess science and math readiness, identify skill gaps, and give a very, very clear picture to the parent as well as student about the child's readiness in those subjects. - Use Case 2 (IBDP / A-Level Predicted-grade recovery): Applications often depend on grades, and that's where exactly students end up struggling in the first one and a half year in their DP or the A-Level programs. The student marks might be inconsistent in tests, maybe facing some challenges in terms of writing the answers as per the mark schemes, unsure on how to prioritize and what to prioritize before their mock or predicted grades. In our approach, we follow a 6-week academic recovery sprint, which includes diagnostics, topic prioritization, timed practice, feedback, and mock review. Honestly, we do not promise any grade miracles—that's not going to be possible—but what we build is a measurable academic control with the student and the parent, so that all of the stakeholders know what is improving and what still needs to be worked on. - Use Case 3 (STEM profile evidence): This is again not a very major segment of ours, but yes, we do some part of in-house support towards STEM in terms of product and prototyping, in terms of research papers and other areas of STEM. We've been working with some TOC members already who have been instrumental in shaping the research part of the execution as well as documentation. For counselors, if you see this is a very strong story, that in case if you want a student to excel not just academically but with a STEM profile evidence as well, we can primarily work in harmony together to create that.

Himansshu Jainn: So let's have a quick diagnostic poll with all of you. Let's say that you have a Grade 10 student and he wants to do engineering. Math is strong in classwork, but weak in timed problem-solving. Physics concepts are also very good understood verbally, but it lacks exam answering structure. What do you think should be diagnosed first? - A: Concept clarity - B: Exam confidence - C: Parent uncertainty - D: Profile-subject mismatch

Himansshu Jainn: I request all of you to just put your answers as A, B, C, or D in the chat box. That will primarily give us a fair interaction with one another as well. Let's take about a 30-second pause at the moment.
Himansshu Jainn: [silence/waiting for responses]

Himansshu Jainn: All right. Yes, thanks to a few of you who have managed to send in your answers. So my view primarily obviously supports with the idea that the student may need both concept-to-exam transition, as well as the timed problem-solving diagnosis. So the issue is not necessarily intelligence; the issue is primarily whether the learning is converting into exam performance. This is exactly why diagnostics generally matter before families start taking high-pressure academic decisions as well.

Himansshu Jainn: Now what could success primarily look out for TOC members, or for counselors to be more precise: - For counselors: Clear academic risk picture, stronger subject-fit evidence, better predicted-grade visibility, more credible application narrative, less parent confusion. - For school leaders: Structured support for underperformers, stronger parent communication, improved student preparedness, external academic reinforcement respecting school systems. - For university partners: Stronger subject commitment, academic depth before enrollment, profile evidence aligned to intended course, reduced first-year attrition risk.

Himansshu Jainn: And this is how we define satisfaction at TSS: - Student Confidence (The internal signal): Concept clarity, homework completion, test performance, and willingness to attempt harder questions. - Parent Clarity (The visibility loop): Transparent roadmap, progress summaries, next steps, and realistic expectations. - Counselor Trust (The handoff): Concise academic summary that helps subject choice, profile strategy, and application planning. - University Readiness (The outward proof): Evidence of academic intent, subject depth, and preparedness for the next stage. - Tracked in practice: Baseline score, topic tracker, homework quality, mock review, confidence note, parent feedback.

Himansshu Jainn: So I would like to propose a partnership model for the 2026–27 intake: 1. Identify: Student has academic or subject-readiness uncertainty risk. 2. Diagnose: TSS conducts academic-fit conversation and baseline mapping. 3. Roadmap: Family receives intervention plan and expected milestones. 4. Report: Progress summary to parent, counselor, and school for clarity.

Himansshu Jainn: The best-fit referrals primarily are the IBDP, IGCSE, MYP, or A-Level students who need subject clarity, diagnostic support, grade readiness, the internal assessment or extended essay help, to a very small extent STEM profile evidence as well.

Himansshu Jainn: So yes, that's the primary focus on. Jyoti Puneet Jolly: But within seven days, Himansshu, can you train them for how the IB evaluate actually? And if there is so much of assistance in, you know, extended essays and IAs, are we actually achieving the learning objectives which IB aims at? You know, we are feeding the mind, we are giving them—we are hand-holding every single step of it. What happens to the inner learning journey of the student?

Himansshu Jainn: Right, right. So see, frankly speaking, I'll come to each question one at a time. So yes, agree to the fact that seven days may not sound relevant to have a complete teacher training program. But the teachers who are hired primarily do not have challenges with the academic content. How it has to be delivered into a classroom set of where the student-teacher ratio is 6:1, how personalization has to be created, how to identify the gaps, what are our benchmark of mapping the student journey is what the training is provided to them. That's one thing.

Himansshu Jainn: Second, with IAs and extended essays, our hand-holding is only towards a facilitating process. We do not write the IAs, we do not write the extended essays. So if at all a child wants to understand "How do I finalize a research question which is not going to be rejected by a school teacher?", we help them towards brainstorming and identifying a research question. Now what's the structure of writing the extended essay, what's the structure of writing an IA is what we do. We do provide them only one feedback after that too they receive from the school. The entire journey has been mapped in a way that the school teacher and the student has to be majorly involved. My job is primarily to just give them some suggestions on giving a checklist: that these are the basics you need, these are the minimum you need in case if you're aiming for a 20 and above in your IA, so you need to meet up all these checklists. So we provide only the blueprint of that and a bit of mentorship, but we do not engage in writing it completely.
Jyoti Puneet Jolly: Okay. My next question is, you know, over a period of 6 months or 8 months with you, how much on an average is the point improvements in Math AA HL or Physics or Chemistry?

Himansshu Jainn: Right. So see, frankly speaking, this might sound a little bit of exaggeration at the moment about us, but our results generally right from the beginning, we have managed to keep it either towards 6 or a 7.
